newsitem.title: USA: U.S. law firm settles age discrimination suit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. law firm settles age discrimination suit.

text.p: The law firm of Pillsbury Madison & Sutro reached a settlement with eight women former employees who sued the firm for alleged age discrimination, both sides said on Wednesday.
The women, who mostly worked as secretaries and are all over 50 years old, alleged that Pillsbury Madison & Sutro gave them poor job performance reviews to force them to retire early.

Their lawyers alleged that the firm was seeking to change its image and wanted its secretaries to look "young and perky." The lawsuit, filed in 1995, alleged that the firm's actions violated California laws barring companies from discriminating because of age.
The law firm denied the charge and said it strictly enforced a non-discrimination policy.
The settlement was reached on Tuesday as jury selection was set to begin in a trial of the claims of one of the women in San Francisco County Superior Court, a lawyer for the plaintiffs said.
A judge had dismissed four of the women from the suit because they accepted an early retirement package from the firm, but that decision was being appealed.
The settlement applied to all eight of the women, who have left the law firm, their lawyers said.
Terms of the settlement were not announced.
Pillsbury Madison & Sutro, headquartered in San Francisco, has six offices in California as well as offices in New York, Washington, D.C., Tokyo and Hong Kong. It employs about 575 attorneys.

"Our clients are pleased with the terms of the settlement. They feel that justice was done and are happy that the case is now finally resolved so that they can move on with their lives," the women's lawyers, Gary Gwilliam and Steven Schectman, said in a statement.
"Our clients showed great courage and determination in this long and difficult lawsuit," they said.
Pillsbury Madison & Sutro said the firm strongly believed that all of its actions were lawful but it was pleased that the case "was finally settled and behind all of us."

One of the plaintiffs was Shirley McCarley, former human resources manager at Pillsbury's San Francisco office. McCarley testified that she was ordered to force older secretaries to retire so the firm could hire younger women.
After raising questions about the policy, McCarley testified that her bosses suggested she might be happier working elsewhere, according to news reports.
